To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the biological markers of depression, anxiety, and alcoholism are the same, namely, the same biological markers as those for strain.

the biological markers of the stress response (e.g., plasma cortisol and catecholamine levels, plasma prolactin levels) are increased in depressed patients and that the biological markers for the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis (e.g., TSH levels) are decreased.

the biological markers described so far in the literature for the major psychiatric disorders cannot be considered as biological indicators of the pathophysiology of the disorder, because none of them fulfills the criteria proposed in this paper.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of biological markers that are valid and specific for a psychiatric disorder.
the development of biological markers of strain and stress and the elucidation of the pathogenetic role of the aspecific stress response in mental disorders.
the identification and validation of biological markers of strain and stress, and of anxiety and depression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
biological markers are at the moment not useful in psychiatry.
the biological markers in the literature are not yet sufficiently specific to serve as biological markers of psychiatric disorders.
biological markers are not available for the psychiatric disorders mentioned above, and that they cannot be expected in the near future.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the search for biological markers in psychiatry is not yet successful, but that the concept of biological markers is useful and should be pursued.
biological markers in psychiatry do not exist, and if they do, they are of no clinical relevance for the diagnosis or the treatment of psychiatric disorders.
the search for biological markers for the major psychiatric disorders is premature.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the current biological markers for depression, schizophrenia and anxiety are not specific for the disorder, but rather for the aspecific processes involved in the pathophysiology and pathogenesis of all stress-related disorders.
we should be careful in the use of the term "biological markers" in psychiatry.
we need to develop new biological markers that are sensitive to specific pathophysiological, pathogenetic and etiologic factors of psychiatric disorders.
